questions.question: Define fracture as a mode of structural failure, explain the difference between brittle and ductile failure, and give two cures for a lack of strength in a model.
questions.expected_answer: Fracture is failure by breaking, snapping, tearing or crushing because a material or joint was asked to carry more force than its strength allows. Brittle materials (glass, chalk, cast iron) fail suddenly with little warning; ductile materials (mild steel, copper, most plastics) stretch and deform visibly before breaking, giving warning. Fatigue is fracture after many repeated small loads. Cures: more or stronger material at the weak point (dowel instead of straw, doubled card), and larger joints with glued tabs, overlaps or gussets since most model fractures occur at joints.

questions.question: Distinguish strength from stiffness, describe bending and buckling, and give the cure for each.
questions.expected_answer: Strength is the ability to carry load without breaking; stiffness is the ability to hold shape without deforming too much, and a structure can be strong but not stiff. Bending is gradual curving of a member under a load across it; cured by depth (card on edge, channel or box sections) and by triangulation. Buckling is the sudden sideways bowing of a long thin member in compression at a load far below its crushing strength; cured by shortening the unbraced length with bracing, by using fatter or tubular sections, or by redesigning so the member is in tension.

questions.question: Explain what makes a structure stable, describe how toppling occurs, and state why adding weight to the top of a structure does not help.
questions.expected_answer: Stability depends on a wide base, a low centre of gravity and weight concentrated near the ground, plus anchoring to the ground. Toppling occurs when a sideways force, such as wind or a hand on a crank, tilts the structure until its centre of gravity passes outside the edge of its base, so the whole structure falls over without any member breaking or bending. Weight at the top raises the centre of gravity and gives the sideways force a longer lever, so it makes toppling more likely; weight belongs low in the base.
